details:
**"What a Wonderful World"**
Armstrong's 1967 recording of the optimistic ballad by Bob Thiele and George David Weiss, sung in his signature gravelly voice. It opens "I see trees of green, red roses too" and later describes "skies of blue and clouds of white," "friends shaking hands, saying how do you do" who are "really saying I love you," and hearing "babies cry." It is the most common giveaway for him.

**"Heebie Jeebies"**
A 1926 Hot Five recording of a Boyd Atkins song, often credited with popularizing (and sometimes said to "invent") scat singing, the improvised singing of wordless syllables. According to legend, Armstrong dropped his lyric sheet during the recording session and began scatting to cover the gap, although scat singing actually predates the recording.

**Hot Five and Hot Seven**
The studio bands Armstrong led for Okeh Records in Chicago from 1925 to 1928, whose recordings shifted jazz from collective ensemble improvisation toward virtuosic individual solos. Members included clarinetist Johnny Dodds and Armstrong's second wife, pianist Lil Hardin, with whom he wrote songs like "My Heart"; Earl Hines later replaced her on piano. Critic Gunther Schuller called Armstrong "the first great soloist" in jazz.

**"West End Blues"**
A King Oliver composition that Armstrong recorded in 1928 with a band including Earl Hines, Fred Robinson, and Jimmy Strong. It opens with a famous unaccompanied virtuoso trumpet cadenza, includes a wordless scat chorus traded with clarinet, and features a long-held high note near the end; it is often called one of the greatest jazz recordings.

**King Oliver**
Joe "King" Oliver, Armstrong's mentor from New Orleans, brought him to Chicago in 1922 to play second cornet in King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band. Armstrong later recorded Oliver's compositions "West End Blues" and "Weather Bird." In 1924 he left to join Fletcher Henderson's orchestra in New York.

**"Hello, Dolly!"**
Armstrong's 1964 cover of the title song of Jerry Herman's Broadway musical, in which he inserted his own name ("This is Louis, Dolly") and sang that Dolly will never go away again and "it's so nice to have you back where you belong." It reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, displacing the Beatles and making him the oldest artist to top the chart at the time; it also titled his album Hello, Dolly!

**"Potato Head Blues"**
A 1927 Hot Seven recording famous for Armstrong's dramatic stop-time trumpet solo, in which the band plays only short chords on the first beats while he improvises in between. It also features a long clarinet solo by Johnny Dodds.

**"Weather Bird"**
A 1928 duet recording of a King Oliver composition with pianist Earl "Fatha" Hines, regarded as a landmark of jazz improvisation for its intricate interplay between trumpet and piano. Armstrong had earlier recorded it with Oliver's band. He and Hines later recorded a famous live "Honeysuckle Rose" in Pasadena in 1951.

**Ella Fitzgerald collaborations**
Armstrong recorded a series of albums with Ella Fitzgerald for Verve in the 1950s, including Ella and Louis and a 1959 album of songs from George Gershwin's opera Porgy and Bess. Their notable duets include "Summertime" and "They Can't Take That Away from Me."

**"Satchmo," New Orleans, and "When the Saints Go Marching In"**
Armstrong was born in New Orleans and nicknamed "Satchmo" (from "Satchel Mouth") and "Pops." His popular recording of the spiritual "When the Saints Go Marching In" strengthened that song's association with New Orleans jazz.

**"Mack the Knife"**
Armstrong's hit 1955 jazz version of "The Ballad of Mack the Knife" from Kurt Weill and Bertolt Brecht's The Threepenny Opera helped make it a jazz standard. Ella Fitzgerald's 1960 live recording in Berlin name-checks both Armstrong and Bobby Darin, who also had a hit with the song.

**The Real Ambassadors**
A 1962 jazz musical created by Dave and Iola Brubeck, inspired by Armstrong's role as a State Department "jazz ambassador" touring the world. Armstrong starred on the recording, singing the civil rights-themed lines "They say I look like God / Could God be black?"

**Hoagy Carmichael songs**
Armstrong had successful re-workings of Hoagy Carmichael's "Stardust," in which he added the improvised words "Oh, memory" before an instrumental break, and "Lazy River."

**The All Stars**
The small band Armstrong led from 1947 onward, after the big-band era, which included trombonists Jack Teagarden and Trummy Young. He performed hits such as "Hello, Dolly!" and "What a Wonderful World" in this later phase of his career.

**French songs and other recordings**
Armstrong recorded popular versions of Édith Piaf's "La Vie en Rose" (arranged with Sy Oliver) and "C'est si bon," which he heard at the 1948 Nice Jazz Festival. Other recordings include "(I'll Be Glad When You're Dead) You Rascal You," "Gone Fishin'" with Bing Crosby, a 1954 album of W. C. Handy songs, and an initially unbilled appearance on Jimmie Rodgers's "Blue Yodel No. 9."
